references.text: The same message about letting the people of Israel go free to serve God in the wilderness was given to Moses at the burning bush.
Moses and Aaron presented the same demand to Pharaoh: 'Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival for me in the wilderness.'
The God of the Hebrews is mentioned again in connection with the demand to let the people go out into the wilderness.
God promised that the people would serve him on this mountain after their deliverance from Egypt.
God commanded Moses to tell Pharaoh to let his son (Israel) go free to serve him.
The same wording is repeated: 'the God of the Hebrews' and the demand, 'Let my people go, so that they may serve me.'
Again, the expression 'the God of the Hebrews' is used with the same demand to let the people go free.
The God of the Hebrews repeats the demand and asks how long Pharaoh will refuse to humble himself.
Stephen quotes God's words to Moses about sending him to Egypt to deliver the people.
Moses left Egypt in faith and did not fear the king's anger, which connects to the confrontation with Pharaoh.
Links Pharaoh's specific resistance to the general prophetic theme that the people consistently refuse to listen to God's messengers.
Highlights Pharaoh's resistance as an example of the broader historical pattern where Israel consistently refuses to listen to God's messengers.
Connects the consequence of refusing to heed God's call (the plagues in Exodus) with the final judgment on Judah in Jeremiah.
Highlights Pharaoh's specific resistance as an expression of the broader biblical theme of Israel's constant rebellion against God.
